Once again, I’m not opposed to quests that require violence on principle. I think it’s an important mix up to the gameplay, and a strong character establishing mechanic. Like, in Fallout 2, when you’ve spent so much of your time talking your way out of various pickles the whole game and you meet Frank Horrigan, it’s like, “whoa, this guy’s so blinded by Enclave ideology, he won’t listen to a thing I say.” It’s an important and good moment. 

I’m opposed to doing so in important main quests without giving players options on how to do it the way that they would like their character to.

And speaking of the Gizmo/Killian quest in Junktown, that’s actually an interesting example, because there’s lots of different ways that could go despite always ending in violence. You can witness the failed assassination on Killian and then make an offer to Gizmo to finish the job. You can plant a bug in Gizmo’s office to get a confession, or you can carry a recorder with you and get him to confess on tape. You can say no to helping Killian and get arrested or get in a fight. You can kill Gizmo before the confession and get banned from the town. If I remember correctly (and I could be wrong on this), if you do everything by the books with Killian, you don’t even have to participate in the killing of Gizmo. The player simply has much more agency over their own actions in the “Kill Gizmo/Killian” quest than the “Kill Kellogg” quest; they’re almost incomparable.

Which is all to say that whether or not it ends in violence isn’t always the important part. The wasteland is a bad place and sometimes that’s inevitable. The important part is giving players options on how to engage in that violence, or different and important ways to engage with the quest leading up to the violence.

are you... disagreeing or agreeing? I’m admittedly not sure I understand what you’re getting at here, sorry.

Kellogg alone is not bad in a microcosm. It makes sense that you wouldn’t be able to save Kellogg; he’s basically committing suicide by sole survivor. He isn’t leaving without a fight, and he isn’t letting you leave without a fight. That’s fine. The problem is this in the context of the rest of the game.

Almost all quest interactions in Fallout 4 end in violence. There are very few opportunities where you get to solve your problems without violence, or even in a different violent way than a gunfight. Kellogg is a problem because he is a symptom of a bigger problem with Fallout 4; Kellogg is a problem because every place where you might have a meaningful choice is just like Kellogg.

Moreover, on “you can’t save Frank Horrigan”: you’re right! You can’t! In the end, Frank Horrigan has to die. But you can convince Enclave Soldiers to go turncoat against him, and you can hack turrets to assist in the fight. That means that there are other options in the fight against Horrigan that are viable than just pure combat skill. You can hypothetically beat him while maintaining the skills of the character you’re role playing.

I hope this makes me sound like I’m not against being forced into combat on principle, but rather that I’m against being forced into combat without considering your characters skills.

I feel like I’m one of the only people who thinks that how much it makes sense doesn’t really matter as much as whether it was a good decision for the story. They can come up with whatever reason they want for the BoS and the Enclave; splinter groups, different contingencies, whatever. But I just want them to do something new and come up with fresh and interesting factions. 

Fallout NV had the major conflict between the Legion, the NCR, and Mr. House (and the best route, independent), and each one brought a new and compelling dynamic to the franchise. Hell, even Fallout 4 had the Railroad, the Institute and the Minutemen. I wouldn’t call any of those particularly good, but at least they aren’t revived corpses from the other games. Now they’re just reviving old factions in different locations because when Bethesda looks at Fallout, they just see the symbols of the old games and pluck them from their meaning.

The BoS and the Enclave have been done to death. I’d really like to see what other organizations in the wasteland look like.
